\"Menelaus\") and [Meriones](./Meriones_(mythology) \"Meriones (mythology)\") lifting [Patroclus](./Patroclus \"Patroclus\")\\'s corpse on a cart while Odysseus looks on, [Etruscan](./Etruscan_art \"Etruscan art\") [alabaster](./Alabaster \"Alabaster\") urn from [Volterra](./Volterra \"Volterra\"), Italy, 2nd century BC\\n\\nOdysseus is represented as one of the most influential Greek champions during the Trojan War in Homer\\'s account. Along with [Nestor](./Nestor_(mythology) \"Nestor (mythology)\") and [Idomeneus](./Idomeneus \"Idomeneus\") he is one of the most trusted counsellors and advisors. He always champions the Achaean cause, especially when others question Agamemnon\\'s command, as in one instance when [Thersites](./Thersites \"Thersites\") speaks against him. When Agamemnon, to test the morale of the Achaeans, announces his intentions to depart Troy, Odysseus restores order to the Greek camp.[[37]](./Odysseus#cite_note-37) Later on, after many of the heroes leave the battlefield due to injuries (including Odysseus and Agamemnon), Odysseus once again persuades Agamemnon not to withdraw. Along with two other envoys, he is chosen in the failed embassy to try to persuade Achilles to return to combat.[[38]](./Odysseus#cite_note-38)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Rhesos_MNA_Naples.jpg/250px-Rhesos_MNA_Naples.jpg)](./File:Rhesos_MNA_Naples.jpg)\\n\\nOdysseus and [Diomedes](./Diomedes \"Diomedes\") stealing the horses of Thracian king [Rhesus](./Rhesus_of_Thrace \"Rhesus of Thrace\") they have just killed. Apulian red-figure situla, from Ruvo\\n\\nWhen [Hector](./Hector \"Hector\") proposes a single combat duel, Odysseus is one of the [Danaans](./Danaans \"Danaans\") who reluctantly volunteered to battle him. [Telamonian Ajax](./Ajax_the_Great \"Ajax the Great\") (\"The Greater\"), however, is the volunteer who eventually fights Hector.[[39]](./Odysseus#cite_note-39) Odysseus aids [Diomedes](./Diomedes \"Diomedes\") during the night operations to kill [Rhesus](./Rhesus_of_Thrace \"Rhesus of Thrace\"), because it had been foretold that if his horses drank from the [Scamander River](./Karamenderes_River \"Karamenderes River\"), Troy could not be taken.[[40]](./Odysseus#cite_note-40)\\n\\nAfter [Patroclus](./Patroclus \"Patroclus\") is slain, it is Odysseus who counsels Achilles to let the [Achaean](./Achaea_(ancient_region) \"Achaea (ancient region)\") men eat and rest rather than follow his rage-driven desire to go back on the offensive—and kill Trojans—immediately. Eventually (and reluctantly), he consents.[[41]](./Odysseus#cite_note-41) During the funeral games for Patroclus, Odysseus becomes involved in a wrestling match with Ajax \"The Greater\" and foot race with Ajax \"The Lesser\", son of Oileus and Nestor\\'s son [Antilochus](./Antilochus \"Antilochus\"). He draws the wrestling match, and with the help of the goddess [Athena](./Athena \"Athena\"), he wins the race.[[42]](./Odysseus#cite_note-42)\\n\\nOdysseus has traditionally been viewed as Achilles\\'s antithesis in the *Iliad*:[[43]](./Odysseus#cite_note-43) while Achilles\\'s anger is all-consuming and of a self-destructive nature, Odysseus is frequently viewed as a man of the mean, a voice of reason, renowned for his self-restraint and diplomatic skills. He is also in some respects antithetical to Telamonian Ajax (Shakespeare\\'s \"beef-witted\" Ajax): while the latter has only brawn to recommend him, Odysseus is not only ingenious (as evidenced by his idea for the Trojan Horse), but an eloquent speaker, a skill perhaps best demonstrated in the embassy to Achilles in book 9 of the *Iliad*. The two are not only foils in the abstract but often opposed in practice since they have many duels and run-ins.\\n\\n#### Other stories from the Trojan War\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/05-Mosaico_del_Oecus._Aquiles_en_Skyros_alta.jpg/250px-05-Mosaico_del_Oecus._Aquiles_en_Skyros_alta.jpg)](./File:05-Mosaico_del_Oecus._Aquiles_en_Skyros_alta.jpg)\\n\\n[Roman mosaic](./Roman_mosaic \"Roman mosaic\") depicting Odysseus at Skyros unveiling the disguised [Achilles](./Achilles \"Achilles\");[[44]](./Odysseus#cite_note-44) from [La Olmeda](./La_Olmeda \"La Olmeda\"), [Pedrosa de la Vega](./Pedrosa_de_la_Vega \"Pedrosa de la Vega\"), Spain, 5th century AD\\n\\nSince a prophecy suggested that the Trojan War would not be won without [Achilles](./Achilles \"Achilles\"), Odysseus and several other [Achaean](./Achaeans_(Homer) \"Achaeans (Homer)\") leaders are described in the *[Achilleid](./Achilleid \"Achilleid\")* as having gone to [Skyros](./Achilles_on_Skyros \"Achilles on Skyros\") to find him. Odysseus discovered Achilles by offering gifts, adornments and musical instruments as well as weapons, to the king\\'s daughters, and then having his companions imitate the noises of an enemy\\'s attack on the island (most notably, making a blast of a trumpet heard), which prompted Achilles to reveal himself by picking a weapon to fight back, and together they departed for the Trojan War.[[45]](./Odysseus#cite_note-45)\\n\\nThe story of the death of [Palamedes](./Palamedes_(mythology) \"Palamedes (mythology)\") has many versions. According to some, Odysseus never forgives Palamedes for unmasking his [feigned madness](./Feigned_madness \"Feigned madness\") and plays a part in his downfall. One tradition says Odysseus convinces a Trojan captive to write a letter pretending to be from Palamedes. A sum of gold is mentioned to have been sent as a reward for Palamedes\\'s treachery. Odysseus then kills the prisoner and hides the gold in Palamedes\\'s tent. He ensures that the letter is found and acquired by Agamemnon, and also gives hints directing the Argives to the gold. This is evidence enough for the Greeks, and they have Palamedes stoned to death. Other sources say that Odysseus and Diomedes goad Palamedes into descending a well with the prospect of treasure being at the bottom. When Palamedes reaches the bottom, the two proceed to bury him with stones, killing him.[[46]](./Odysseus#cite_note-46)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Odysseus_Ajax_Louvre_F340.jpg/250px-Odysseus_Ajax_Louvre_F340.jpg)](./File:Odysseus_Ajax_Louvre_F340.jpg)\\n\\nOinochoe, *ca* 520 BC, Odysseus and [Ajax](./Ajax_the_Great \"Ajax the Great\") fighting over the armour of Achilles\\n\\nWhen Achilles is slain in battle by [Paris](./Paris_(mythology) \"Paris (mythology)\"), it is Odysseus and [Ajax](./Ajax_the_Great \"Ajax the Great\") who retrieve the fallen warrior\\'s body and armour in the thick of heavy fighting. During the funeral games for Achilles, Odysseus competes once again with Ajax. Thetis says that the arms of Achilles will go to the bravest of the Greeks, but only these two warriors dare lay claim to that title. The two Argives became embroiled in a heavy dispute about one another\\'s merits to receive the reward. The Greeks dither out of fear in deciding a winner, because they did not want to insult one and have him abandon the war effort. [Nestor](./Nestor_(mythology) \"Nestor (mythology)\") suggests that they allow the captive Trojans to decide the winner.[[47]](./Odysseus#cite_note-47) The accounts of the *Odyssey* disagree, suggesting that the Greeks themselves hold a secret vote.[[48]](./Odysseus#cite_note-48) In any case, Odysseus is the winner. Enraged and humiliated, Ajax is driven mad by Athena. When he returns to his senses, in shame at how he has slaughtered livestock in his madness, Ajax kills himself by the sword that Hector had given him after their duel.[[49]](./Odysseus#cite_note-49)\\n\\nTogether with Diomedes, Odysseus fetches Achilles\\'s son, [Pyrrhus](./Neoptolemus \"Neoptolemus\"), to come to the aid of the Achaeans, because an oracle had stated that Troy could not be taken without him. A great warrior, Pyrrhus is also called Neoptolemus (Greek for \"new warrior\"). Upon the success of the mission, Odysseus gives Achilles\\'s armour to him.\\n\\nIt is learned that the war can not be won without the poisonous arrows of [Heracles](./Heracles \"Heracles\"), which are owned by the abandoned [Philoctetes](./Philoctetes \"Philoctetes\"). Odysseus and Diomedes (or, according to some accounts, Odysseus and [Neoptolemus](./Neoptolemus \"Neoptolemus\")) leave to retrieve them. Upon their arrival, Philoctetes (still suffering from the wound) is seen still to be enraged at the [Danaans](./Danaans \"Danaans\"), especially at Odysseus, for abandoning him. Although his first instinct is to shoot Odysseus, his anger is eventually defused by Odysseus\\'s persuasive powers and the influence of the gods. Odysseus returns to the Argive camp with Philoctetes and his arrows.[[50]](./Odysseus#cite_note-50)\\n\\nPerhaps Odysseus\\'s most famous contribution to the Greek war effort is devising the strategy of the [Trojan Horse](./Trojan_Horse \"Trojan Horse\"), which allows the Greek army to sneak into Troy under cover of darkness. It is built by [Epeius](./Epeius_of_Phocis \"Epeius of Phocis\") and filled with Greek warriors, led by Odysseus.[[51]](./Odysseus#cite_note-51) Odysseus and Diomedes steal the [Palladium](./Palladium_(mythology) \"Palladium (mythology)\") that lay within Troy\\'s walls, for the Greeks were told they could not sack the city without it. Some late Roman sources indicate that Odysseus schemed to kill his partner on the way back, but Diomedes thwarts this attempt.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Wall_painting_-_rape_of_the_palladion_-_Pompeii_%28I_2_26%29_-_Napoli_MAN_109751_-_02.jpg/250px-Wall_painting_-_rape_of_the_palladion_-_Pompeii_%28I_2_26%29_-_Napoli_MAN_109751_-_02.jpg)](./File:Wall_painting_-_rape_of_the_palladion_-_Pompeii_(I_2_26)_-_Napoli_MAN_109751_-_02.jpg)\\n\\nOdysseus ([pileus hat](./Pileus_(hat) \"Pileus (hat)\")) carrying off the [palladion](./Palladion \"Palladion\") from [Troy](./Troy \"Troy\"), with the help of [Diomedes](./Diomedes \"Diomedes\"), against the resistance of [Cassandra](./Cassandra \"Cassandra\") and other Trojans. Antique fresco from Pompeii.\\n\\n#### \"Cruel, deceitful Ulixes\" of the Romans\\n\\nHomer\\'s *Iliad* and *Odyssey* portray Odysseus as a [culture hero](./Culture_hero \"Culture hero\"), but the Romans, who believed themselves the heirs of Prince [Aeneas](./Aeneas \"Aeneas\") of Troy, considered him a villainous falsifier. In [Virgil](./Virgil \"Virgil\")\\'s *[Aeneid](./Aeneid \"Aeneid\")*, written between 29 and 19 BC, he is constantly referred to as \"cruel Odysseus\" ([Latin](./Latin \"Latin\") *dirus Ulixes*) or \"deceitful Odysseus\" (*pellacis*, *fandi fictor*). Turnus, in *Aeneid*, book 9, reproaches the Trojan Ascanius with images of rugged, forthright Latin virtues, declaring (in [John Dryden](./John_Dryden \"John Dryden\")\\'s translation), \"You shall not find the sons of Atreus here, nor need the frauds of sly Ulysses fear.\" While the Greeks admired his cunning and deceit, these qualities did not recommend themselves to the Romans, who possessed a rigid sense of honour. In Euripides\\'s tragedy *[Iphigenia at Aulis](./Iphigenia_at_Aulis \"Iphigenia at Aulis\")*, having convinced Agamemnon to consent to the sacrifice of his daughter, Iphigenia, to appease the goddess [Artemis](./Artemis \"Artemis\"), Odysseus facilitates the immolation by telling Iphigenia\\'s mother, [Clytemnestra](./Clytemnestra \"Clytemnestra\"), that the girl is to be wed to [Achilles](./Achilles \"Achilles\"). Odysseus\\'s attempts to avoid his sacred oath to defend [Menelaus](./Menelaus \"Menelaus\") and [Helen](./Helen_of_Troy \"Helen of Troy\") offended Roman notions of duty, and the many stratagems and tricks that he employed to get his way offended Roman notions of honour.\\n\\n### Journey home to Ithaca\\n\\nFurther information: [Homer\\'s Ithaca](./Homer\\'s_Ithaca \"Homer\\'s Ithaca\") and [Returns from Troy](./Returns_from_Troy \"Returns from Troy\")\\n\\nOdysseus is probably best known as the eponymous hero of the *Odyssey*. This epic describes his travels, which lasted for 10 years, as he tries to return home after the Trojan War and reassert his place as rightful king of Ithaca.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Arnold_B%C3%B6cklin_-_Odysseus_and_Polyphemus.jpg/250px-Arnold_B%C3%B6cklin_-_Odysseus_and_Polyphemus.jpg)](./File:Arnold_Böcklin_-_Odysseus_and_Polyphemus.jpg)\\n\\n*[Odysseus and Polyphemus](./Odysseus_and_Polyphemus_(Böcklin) \"Odysseus and Polyphemus (Böcklin)\")* (1896) by [Arnold Böcklin](./Arnold_Böcklin \"Arnold Böcklin\"): Odysseus and his crew escape the Cyclops [Polyphemus](./Polyphemus \"Polyphemus\").\\n\\nHomebound from Troy, after a raid on [Ismarus](./Ismara \"Ismara\") in the land of the [Cicones](./Cicones \"Cicones\"), he and his twelve ships are driven off course by storms. They visit the lethargic [Lotus-Eaters](./Lotus-eaters \"Lotus-eaters\") and are captured by the [Cyclops](./Cyclopes \"Cyclopes\") [Polyphemus](./Polyphemus \"Polyphemus\") while visiting his island. After Polyphemus eats several of his men, he and Odysseus have a discussion and Odysseus tells Polyphemus his name is [Outis](./Outis \"Outis\") (\"Nobody\"). Odysseus takes a barrel of wine and the Cyclops drinks it, falling asleep. Odysseus and his men take a wooden stake, ignite it with the remaining wine, and blind him. While they escape, Polyphemus cries in pain, and the other Cyclopes ask him what is wrong. Polyphemus cries, \"Nobody has blinded me!\" and the other Cyclopes think he has gone mad. Odysseus and his crew escape, but Odysseus rashly reveals his real name, and Polyphemus prays to Poseidon, his father, to take revenge. They stay with [Aeolus](./Aeolus_(son_of_Hippotes) \"Aeolus (son of Hippotes)\"), the master of the winds, who gives Odysseus a leather bag containing all the winds, except the west wind, a gift that should have ensured a safe return home. However, the sailors foolishly open the bag while Odysseus sleeps, thinking that it contains gold. All of the winds fly out, and the resulting storm drives the ships back the way they had come, just as Ithaca comes into sight.[[52]](./Odysseus#cite_note-52)\\n\\nAfter pleading in vain with Aeolus to help them again, they re-embark and encounter the cannibalistic [Laestrygonians](./Laestrygonians \"Laestrygonians\"). Odysseus\\'s ship is the only one to escape. He sails on and visits the witch-goddess [Circe](./Circe \"Circe\"). She turns half of his men into swine after feeding them cheese and wine. Hermes warns Odysseus about Circe and gives him a drug called [moly](./Moly_(herb) \"Moly (herb)\"), which resists Circe\\'s magic. Circe, being attracted to Odysseus\\'s resistance, falls in love with him and releases his men. Odysseus and his crew remain with her on the island for one year, while they feast and drink. Finally, Odysseus\\'s men convince him to leave for Ithaca.\\n\\nGuided by Circe\\'s instructions, Odysseus and his crew cross the ocean and reach a harbor at the western edge of the world, where Odysseus sacrifices to the dead and [summons the spirit](./Nekuia \"Nekuia\") of the old prophet [Tiresias](./Tiresias \"Tiresias\") for advice. Next Odysseus meets the spirit of his own mother, who had died of grief during his long absence. From her, he learns for the first time news of his own household, threatened by the greed of [Penelope](./Penelope \"Penelope\")\\'s [suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope \"Suitors of Penelope\"). Odysseus also talks to his fallen war comrades and the mortal shade of [Heracles](./Heracles \"Heracles\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Mosa%C3%AFque_d%27Ulysse_et_les_sir%C3%A8nes.jpg/250px-Mosa%C3%AFque_d%27Ulysse_et_les_sir%C3%A8nes.jpg)](./File:Mosaïque_d\\'Ulysse_et_les_sirènes.jpg)\\n\\nOdysseus and the [Sirens](./Siren_(mythology) \"Siren (mythology)\"), Ulixes [mosaic](./Mosaic \"Mosaic\") at the [Bardo National Museum](./Bardo_National_Museum_(Tunis) \"Bardo National Museum (Tunis)\") in [Tunis](./Tunis \"Tunis\"), Tunisia, 2nd century AD\\n\\nOdysseus and his men return to Circe\\'s island, and she advises them on the remaining stages of the journey. They skirt the land of the [Sirens](./Siren_(mythology) \"Siren (mythology)\"), pass between the six-headed monster [Scylla](./Scylla \"Scylla\") and the whirlpool [Charybdis](./Charybdis \"Charybdis\"), where they row directly between the two. However, [Scylla](./Scylla \"Scylla\") drags the boat towards her by grabbing the oars and eats six men.\\n\\nThey land on the island of [Thrinacia](./Thrinacia \"Thrinacia\"). There, Odysseus\\'s men ignore the warnings of Tiresias and Circe and hunt down the sacred cattle of the sun god [Helios](./Helios \"Helios\"). Helios tells [Zeus](./Zeus \"Zeus\") what happened and demands Odysseus\\'s men be punished or else he will take the sun and shine it in the Underworld. Zeus fulfills Helios\\'s demands by causing a shipwreck during a thunderstorm in which all but Odysseus drown. He washes ashore on the island of [Ogygia](./Ogygia \"Ogygia\"), where [Calypso](./Calypso_(mythology) \"Calypso (mythology)\") compels him to remain as her lover for seven years. He finally escapes when [Hermes](./Hermes \"Hermes\") tells Calypso to release Odysseus.[[53]](./Odysseus#cite_note-53)\\n\\nOdysseus is shipwrecked and befriended by the [Phaeacians](./Scheria \"Scheria\"). After he tells them his story, the Phaeacians, led by King [Alcinous](./Alcinous \"Alcinous\"), agree to help Odysseus get home. They deliver him at night, while he is fast asleep, to a hidden harbor on Ithaca. He finds his way to the hut of one of his own former slaves, the swineherd [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus \"Eumaeus\"), and also meets up with his son [Telemachus](./Telemachus \"Telemachus\") returning from Sparta. Athena disguises Odysseus as a wandering beggar to learn how things stand in his household.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/The_return_of_Ulysses.gif/250px-The_return_of_Ulysses.gif)](./File:The_return_of_Ulysses.gif)\\n\\nThe return of Ulysses, illustration by E. M. Synge from the 1909 *Story of the World* children\\'s book series (book 1: *On the shores of Great Sea*)\\n\\nWhen the disguised Odysseus returns after 20 years, he is recognized only by his faithful dog, [Argos](./Argos_(dog) \"Argos (dog)\"). Penelope announces in her long interview with the disguised hero that whoever can string Odysseus\\'s rigid bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axe shafts may have her hand. According to [Bernard Knox](./Bernard_Knox \"Bernard Knox\"), \"For the plot of the *Odyssey*, of course, her decision is the turning point, the move that makes possible the long-predicted triumph of the returning hero\".[[54]](./Odysseus#cite_note-54) Odysseus\\'s identity is discovered by the housekeeper, [Eurycleia](./Eurycleia \"Eurycleia\"), as she is washing his feet and discovers an old scar Odysseus received during a boar hunt. Odysseus swears her to secrecy, threatening to kill her if she tells anyone.\\n\\nWhen the contest of the bow begins, none of the suitors are able to string the bow. After all the suitors have given up, the disguised Odysseus asks to participate. Though the suitors refuse at first, Penelope intervenes and allows the \"stranger\" (the disguised Odysseus) to participate. Odysseus easily strings his bow and wins the contest. Having done so, he proceeds to slaughter the suitors (beginning with Antinous whom he finds drinking from Odysseus\\'s cup) with help from Telemachus and two of Odysseus\\'s servants, [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus \"Eumaeus\") the swineherd and [Philoetius](./Philoetius \"Philoetius\") the cowherd. Odysseus tells the serving women who slept with the suitors to clean up the mess of corpses and then has those women hanged in terror. He tells Telemachus that he will replenish his stocks by raiding nearby islands. Odysseus has now revealed himself in all his glory (with a little makeover by Athena); yet Penelope cannot believe that her husband has really returned—she fears that it is perhaps some god in disguise, as in the story of [Alcmene](./Alcmene \"Alcmene\") (mother of Heracles)—and tests him by ordering her servant Euryclea to move the bed in their wedding-chamber. Odysseus protests that this cannot be done since he made the bed himself and knows that one of its legs is a living [olive tree](./Olive_tree \"Olive tree\"). Penelope finally accepts that he truly is her husband, a moment that highlights their *homophrosýnē* (\"like-mindedness\").\\n\\nThe next day Odysseus and Telemachus visit the country farm of his old father [Laërtes](./Laertes_(father_of_Odysseus) \"Laertes (father of Odysseus)\"). The citizens of Ithaca follow Odysseus on the road, planning to avenge the killing of the Suitors, their sons. The goddess Athena and the god Zeus intervene and persuade both sides to make peace.[[55]](./Odysseus#cite_note-55)\\n\\n### Other tales\\n\\nAccording to some late sources, most of them purely genealogical, Odysseus had many other children besides [Telemachus](./Telemachus \"Telemachus\"). Most such genealogies aimed to link Odysseus with the foundation of many [Italic](./Italy \"Italy\") cities.[[56]](./Odysseus#cite_note-56) This would seem to contradict *The Odyssey*, which says that Odysseus\\'s family line can only produce a single child per generation by the order of Zeus, with Telemachus already existing as that sole heir.[[57]](./Odysseus#cite_note-After_the_Odyssey-57)[[58]](./Odysseus#cite_note-58) However, the *Odyssey* also notes the existence of Odysseus\\'s sister, Ctimene.[[33]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Women_in_Odyssey-33)\\n\\nThe most famous of the other children are:\\n\\n* with [Penelope](./Penelope \"Penelope\"): [Poliporthes](./Poliporthes \"Poliporthes\") (born after Odysseus\\'s return from Troy)\\n* with [Circe](./Circe \"Circe\"): [Telegonus](./Telegonus_(son_of_Odysseus) \"Telegonus (son of Odysseus)\"), [Ardeas](./Ardeas \"Ardeas\"), [Latinus](./Latinus \"Latinus\"), also [Auson](./Auson_(king) \"Auson (king)\") and [Cassiphone](./Cassiphone \"Cassiphone\").[[59]](./Odysseus#cite_note-59) [Xenagoras](./Xenagoras_(historian) \"Xenagoras (historian)\") writes that Odysseus with Circe had three sons, [Romos](./Rhomos \"Rhomos\") ([Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language \"Ancient Greek language\"): Ῥώμος), [Anteias](./Anteias \"Anteias\") ([Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language \"Ancient Greek language\"): Ἀντείας) and [Ardeias](./Ardeias \"Ardeias\") ([Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language \"Ancient Greek language\"): Ἀρδείας), who built three cities and called them after their own names. The city that Romos founded was [Rome](./Rome \"Rome\").[[60]](./Odysseus#cite_note-60)\\n* with [Calypso](./Calypso_(mythology) \"Calypso (mythology)\"): [Nausithous](./Nausithous \"Nausithous\"), [Nausinous](./Nausinous \"Nausinous\")\\n* with [Callidice](./Callidice_of_Thesprotia \"Callidice of Thesprotia\"): [Polypoetes](./Polypoetes \"Polypoetes\")\\n* with [Euippe](./Euippe_(daughter_of_Tyrimmas) \"Euippe (daughter of Tyrimmas)\"): [Euryalus](./Euryalus \"Euryalus\")\\n* with daughter of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) \"Thoas (king of Aetoila)\"): Leontophonus\\n\\nHe figures in the end of the story of King [Telephus](./Telephus \"Telephus\") of [Mysia](./Mysia \"Mysia\").\\n\\nThe last poem in the [Epic Cycle](./Epic_Cycle \"Epic Cycle\") is called the *[Telegony](./Telegony \"Telegony\")*, and is now lost. According to remaining fragments, it told the story of Odysseus\\'s last voyage to the land of the Thesprotians. There he married the queen [Callidice](./Callidice_of_Thesprotia \"Callidice of Thesprotia\"). Then he led the Thesprotians in a war with their neighbors the Brygoi (Brygi, Brygians) and defeated in battle the neighboring peoples who attacked him. When Callidice died, Odysseus returned home to Ithaca, leaving their son, [Polypoetes](./Polypoetes \"Polypoetes\"), to rule Thesprotia.[[61]](./Odysseus#cite_note-CinaethonTelegony-61) Contradicting the reading of Tiresias\\'s prophecy in *The Odyssey* that Odysseus will have a gentle death in old age after making it home,[[57]](./Odysseus#cite_note-After_the_Odyssey-57)[[62]](./Odysseus#cite_note-62) the *Telogony* claims that he met his death at the hands of [Telegonus](./Telegonus_(son_of_Odysseus) \"Telegonus (son of Odysseus)\"), his son with Circe, after a misunderstanding. Telegonus attacked his father with a poisoned, stingray spine-tipped spear, given to him by Circe. Before dying, Odysseus recognized his son. Telegonus then brought back his father\\'s corpse to Aeaea, together with Penelope and Odysseus\\'s son by her, Telemachus. After burying Odysseus, Circe made the other three immortal. Circe married Telemachus, and Telegonus married Penelope[[61]](./Odysseus#cite_note-CinaethonTelegony-61) by the advice of Athena.[[63]](./Odysseus#cite_note-63) An alternative version to Odysseus\\' death by stingray spine was presented in the *Ghost-Raisers*, a lost fifth-century BC tragedy by [Aeschylus](./Aeschylus \"Aeschylus\") inspired by the nekyia episode of the *Odyssey*. In the tragedy, the dead Tiresias predicted that one day a heron\\'s droppings containing said barb would fall upon an aged Odysseus\\' bald head and rot his skin.[[64]](./Odysseus#cite_note-64)\\n\\nAccording to what seems to be later tradition, Odysseus was resurrected by Circe after his death at the hands of Telegonus. Afterward, he married Telemachus to [Cassiphone](./Cassiphone \"Cassiphone\"), the daughter he had with Circe.[[65]](./Odysseus#cite_note-65)[[66]](./Odysseus#cite_note-66) Telemachus however killed Circe after a quarrel, causing Cassiphone to kill him in revenge. Odysseus witnessing those unfortunate events died again, of grief this time.[[67]](./Odysseus#cite_note-67)\\n\\nIn 5th century BC [Athens](./Athens \"Athens\"), tales of the Trojan War were popular subjects for [tragedies](./Tragedies \"Tragedies\"). Odysseus figures centrally or indirectly in a number of the extant plays by [Aeschylus](./Aeschylus \"Aeschylus\"), [Sophocles](./Sophocles \"Sophocles\") (*[Ajax](./Ajax_(Sophocles) \"Ajax (Sophocles)\")*, *[Philoctetes](./Philoctetes_(Sophocles) \"Philoctetes (Sophocles)\")*) and [Euripides](./Euripides \"Euripides\") (*[Hecuba](./Hecuba_(play) \"Hecuba (play)\")*, *[Rhesus](./Rhesus_(play) \"Rhesus (play)\")*, *[Cyclops](./Cyclops_(play) \"Cyclops (play)\")*) and figured in still more that have not survived. In his *Ajax*, Sophocles portrays Odysseus as a modern voice of reasoning compared to the title character\\'s rigid antiquity.\\n\\n[Plato](./Plato \"Plato\") in his dialogue *[Hippias Minor](./Hippias_Minor \"Hippias Minor\")* examines a literary question about whom Homer intended to portray as the better man, Achilles or Odysseus.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Odysseus_-01.jpg/330px-Odysseus_-01.jpg)](./File:Odysseus_-01.jpg)\\n\\nHead of Odysseus wearing a [pileus](./Pileus_(hat) \"Pileus (hat)\") depicted on a 3rd-century BC coin from [Ithaca](./Ithaca_(island) \"Ithaca (island)\")\\n\\n[Pausanias](./Pausanias_(geographer) \"Pausanias (geographer)\") at the *[Description of Greece](./Description_of_Greece \"Description of Greece\")* writes that at [Pheneus](./Pheneus \"Pheneus\") there was a bronze statue of Poseidon, surnamed Hippios ([Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language \"Ancient Greek language\"): Ἵππιος), meaning *of horse*, which according to the legends was dedicated by Odysseus and also a sanctuary of [Artemis](./Artemis \"Artemis\") which was called Heurippa ([Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language \"Ancient Greek language\"): Εὑρίππα), meaning *horse finder*, and was founded by Odysseus.[[68]](./Odysseus#cite_note-perseus.tufts.edu-68) According to the legends Odysseus lost his mares and traversed Greece in search of them. He found them on that site in Pheneus.[[68]](./Odysseus#cite_note-perseus.tufts.edu-68) Pausanias adds that according to the people of Pheneus, when Odysseus found his mares he decided to keep horses in the land of Pheneus, just as he reared his cows. The people of Pheneus also pointed out to him writing, purporting to be instructions of Odysseus to those tending his mares.[[69]](./Odysseus#cite_note-69)\\n\\nAs Ulysses, he is mentioned regularly in [Virgil](./Virgil \"Virgil\")\\'s *[Aeneid](./Aeneid \"Aeneid\")* written between 29 and 19 BC, and the poem\\'s hero, [Aeneas](./Aeneas \"Aeneas\"), rescues one of Ulysses\\'s crew members who was left behind on the island of the Cyclopes. He in turn offers a first-person account of some of the same events Homer relates, in which Ulysses appears directly. Virgil\\'s Ulysses typifies his view of the Greeks: he is cunning but impious, and ultimately malicious and hedonistic.\\n\\n[Ovid](./Ovid \"Ovid\") retells parts of Ulysses\\'s journeys, focusing on his romantic involvements with Circe and Calypso, and recasts him as, in [Harold Bloom](./Harold_Bloom \"Harold Bloom\")\\'s phrase, \"one of the great wandering womanizers\". Ovid also gives a detailed account of the contest between Ulysses and [Ajax](./Ajax_the_Great \"Ajax the Great\") for the armour of Achilles.\\n\\nGreek legend tells of Ulysses as the founder of [Lisbon](./Lisbon \"Lisbon\"), Portugal, calling it *Ulisipo* or *Ulisseya*, during his twenty-year errand on the Mediterranean and Atlantic seas.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] [Olisipo](./Olisipo \"Olisipo\") was Lisbon\\'s name in the Roman Empire. This [folk etymology](./Folk_etymology \"Folk etymology\") is recounted by [Strabo](./Strabo \"Strabo\") based on [Asclepiades of Myrlea](./Asclepiades_of_Myrlea \"Asclepiades of Myrlea\")\\'s words,[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] by [Pomponius Mela](./Pomponius_Mela \"Pomponius Mela\"),[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] by [Gaius Julius Solinus](./Gaius_Julius_Solinus \"Gaius Julius Solinus\") (3rd century AD)[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*], and would later be reiterated by [Camões](./Luís_de_Camões \"Luís de Camões\") in his epic poem *[Os Lusíadas](./Os_Lusíadas \"Os Lusíadas\")* (first printed in 1572).[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nIn one version of Odysseus\\'s end, he is eventually turned into a horse by Athena.[[70]](./Odysseus#cite_note-70)\\n\\nIn post-classical tradition\\n---------------------------\\n\\nOdysseus is one of the most recurrent characters in [Western culture](./Western_culture \"Western culture\").\\n\\n### Middle Ages and Renaissance\\n\\n[Dante Alighieri](./Dante_Alighieri \"Dante Alighieri\"), in the [Canto](./Canto \"Canto\") XXVI of the *[Inferno](./Inferno_(Dante) \"Inferno (Dante)\")* segment of his *[Divine Comedy](./Divine_Comedy \"Divine Comedy\")* (1308–1320), encounters Odysseus (\"Ulisse\" in Italian) near the very bottom of Hell: with [Diomedes](./Diomedes \"Diomedes\"), he walks wrapped in flame in the eighth ring (*Counselors of Fraud*) of the [Eighth Circle](./Malebolge \"Malebolge\") (*Sins of Malice*), as punishment for his schemes and conspiracies that won the Trojan War. In a famous passage, Dante has Odysseus relate a different version of his voyage and death from the one told by Homer. He tells how he set out with his men from Circe\\'s island for a journey of exploration to sail beyond the [Pillars of Hercules](./Pillars_of_Hercules \"Pillars of Hercules\") and into the Western sea to find what adventures awaited them. Men, says Ulisse, are not made to live like brutes, but to follow virtue and knowledge.[[71]](./Odysseus#cite_note-71)\\n\\nAfter travelling west and south for five months, they see in the distance a great mountain rising from the sea (this is [Purgatory](./Purgatory \"Purgatory\"), in Dante\\'s cosmology) before a storm sinks them. Dante did not have access to the original Greek texts of the Homeric epics, so his knowledge of their subject-matter was based only on information from later sources, chiefly [Virgil](./Virgil \"Virgil\")\\'s *[Aeneid](./Aeneid \"Aeneid\")* but also [Ovid](./Ovid \"Ovid\"); hence the discrepancy between Dante and Homer.[[72]](./Odysseus#cite_note-72)\\n\\nHe appears in [Shakespeare](./Shakespeare \"Shakespeare\")\\'s *[Troilus and Cressida](./Troilus_and_Cressida \"Troilus and Cressida\")* (1602), set during the Trojan War.\\n\\n### Modern literature\\n\\n#### Poetry\\n\\nIn her poem [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/20px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png)](./File:Wikisource-logo.svg) [Site of the Castle of Ulysses](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Letitia%20Elizabeth%20Landon%20(L.%20E.%20L.)%20in%20Fisher\\'s%20Drawing%20Room%20Scrap%20Book,%201837/Site%20of%20the%20Castle%20of%20Ulysses \"s:Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L. E. L.) in Fisher\\'s Drawing Room Scrap Book, 1837/Site of the Castle of Ulysses\"). (published in 1836), [Letitia Elizabeth Landon](./Letitia_Elizabeth_Landon \"Letitia Elizabeth Landon\") gives her version of *The Song of the Sirens* with an explanation of its purpose, structure and meaning. This illustrates a painting by [Charles Bentley](./Charles_Bentley_(painter) \"Charles Bentley (painter)\") engraved by R. L.) in Fisher\\'s Drawing Room Scrap Book, 1837/Town and Harbour of Ithaca\"). and harks back to the island \\'where Ulysses was king\\'.[[74]](./Odysseus#cite_note-74)\\n\\n[Alfred, Lord Tennyson](./Alfred,_Lord_Tennyson \"Alfred, Lord Tennyson\")\\'s poem \"[Ulysses](./Ulysses_(poem) \"Ulysses (poem)\")\" (published in 1842) presents an aging king who has seen too much of the world to be happy sitting on a throne idling his days away. Leaving the task of civilizing his people to his son, he gathers together a band of old comrades \"to sail beyond the sunset\".\\n\\n[Nikos Kazantzakis](./Nikos_Kazantzakis \"Nikos Kazantzakis\")\\'s *[The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel](./The_Odyssey:_A_Modern_Sequel \"The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel\")* (1938), a 33,333-line epic poem, begins with Odysseus cleansing his body of the blood of [Penelope](./Penelope \"Penelope\")\\'s suitors. Odysseus soon leaves Ithaca in search of new adventures. Before his death he abducts Helen, incites revolutions in [Crete](./Crete \"Crete\") and [Egypt](./Egypt \"Egypt\"), communes with God, and meets representatives of such famous historical and literary figures as [Lenin](./Lenin \"Lenin\"), [Don Quixote](./Alonso_Quijano \"Alonso Quijano\") and [Jesus](./Jesus_Christ \"Jesus Christ\").\\n\\nIn 1986, Irish poet [Eilean Ni Chuilleanain](./Eilean_Ni_Chuilleanain \"Eilean Ni Chuilleanain\") published \"The Second Voyage\", a poem in which she makes use of the story of Odysseus.\\n\\n#### Novels\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Bay_of_Palaiokastritsa_from_Bellavista.JPG/250px-Bay_of_Palaiokastritsa_from_Bellavista.JPG)](./File:Bay_of_Palaiokastritsa_from_Bellavista.JPG)\\n\\nThe bay of [Palaiokastritsa](./Palaiokastritsa \"Palaiokastritsa\") in [Corfu](./Corfu \"Corfu\") as seen from Bella vista of Lakones, considered to be the place where Odysseus disembarked and met [Nausicaa](./Nausicaa \"Nausicaa\") for the first time. Rivera-Herrans provides the voice of Odysseus.[[83]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Troy_Saga-83)[[84]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Music_Review-84)\\n\\n### Comparative mythology and folkloristics\\n\\nOver time, comparisons between Odysseus and other heroes of different mythologies and religions have been made. A similar story exists in [Hindu mythology](./Hindu_mythology \"Hindu mythology\") with [Nala](./Nala \"Nala\") and [Damayanti](./Damayanti \"Damayanti\") where Nala separates from Damayanti and is reunited with her.[[85]](./Odysseus#cite_note-85) The story of stringing a bow is similar to the description in the *[Ramayana](./Ramayana \"Ramayana\")* of [Rama](./Rama \"Rama\") stringing the bow to win [Sita](./Sita \"Sita\")\\'s hand in marriage.[[86]](./Odysseus#cite_note-86)\\n\\n[Virgil\\'s *Aeneid* has evident similarities](./Parallels_between_Virgil\\'s_Aeneid_and_Homer\\'s_Iliad_and_Odyssey \"Parallels between Virgil\\'s Aeneid and Homer\\'s Iliad and Odyssey\") to the Odyssey. [Virgil](./Virgil \"Virgil\") tells the story of [Aeneas](./Aeneas \"Aeneas\") and his travels to what would become Rome. On his journey he endures strife comparable to that of Odysseus. However, the motives for both of their journeys differ as Aeneas was driven by this sense of duty granted to him by the gods that he must abide by. He keeps in mind the future of his people, fitting for the future *Father of Rome*.\\n\\nIn [folkloristics](./Folkloristics \"Folkloristics\"), the story of Odysseus\\'s journey back to his native Ithaca and wife Penelope corresponds to the tale type ATU 974, [\"The Homecoming Husband\"](./\"The_Homecoming_Husband\"?action=edit&redlink=1 \"\\\\\"The Homecoming Husband\\\\\"\")\\xa0[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heimkehr%20des%20Gatten \"de:Heimkehr des Gatten\")], of the international [Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index](./Aarne–Thompson–Uther_Index \"Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index\") for folktale classification.[[87]](./Odysseus#cite_note-87)[[88]](./Odysseus#cite_note-88)[[89]](./Odysseus#cite_note-89)[[90]](./Odysseus#cite_note-90)\\n\\nRole as a figure of worship\\n---------------------------\\n\\nEvidence suggests the existence of a cult dedicated to Odysseus on Ithaca. This evidence includes public games called the Odysseia (τά Ὀδύσσεια) and a designated public gathering place[[91]](./Odysseus#cite_note-91) or a sanctuary,[[92]](./Odysseus#cite_note-92) known as the Odysseion (τό Ὀδύσσειον).\\nIn 2025, researchers identified what is believed to be the sanctuary of Odysseus at the site Agios Athanasios–School of Homer in northern Ithaca (known since the 19th century as the \"School of Homer\". Two late Hellenistic inscriptions were discovered bearing \"ΟΔΥCCEOC\" (genitive) and \"ΟΔΥCCEI\" (dative). These align with a 1930s inscription from the Polis Bay cave reading \"ΕΥΧΗΝ ΟΔΥCCΕΙ\" (\"Thanks Odysseus\"). Additional finds, such as a miniature bronze bust of Odysseus, 34 clay votive fragments, loom weights, jewelry, and over 100 coins, highlight the site\\'s religious and social role during the Hellenistic and early Roman periods (3rd century BCE – 2nd century CE). The lower terrace, featuring architectural remains, carved dedication niches, and roof tiles inscribed with references to [Apollo](./Apollo \"Apollo\") Agyieus and the symbol \"ΔΗ\" (which may indicate \"public\"), confirms the site\\'s function in formal religious rituals. This indicates that the sanctuary catered to both local devotees and visiting pilgrims.[[93]](./Odysseus#cite_note-93)\\n\\n[Strabo](./Strabo \"Strabo\") writes that on Meninx ([Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language \"Ancient Greek language\"): Μῆνιγξ) island, modern [Djerba](./Djerba \"Djerba\") at [Tunisia](./Tunisia \"Tunisia\"), there was an altar to Odysseus.[[94]](./Odysseus#cite_note-94)\\n\\n[Pliny the Elder](./Pliny_the_Elder \"Pliny the Elder\") writes that in Italy there were some small islands (modern Torricella, Praca, Brace and other rocks)[[95]](./Odysseus#cite_note-95) which were called Ithacesiae because of a watchtower that Odysseus built there.[[96]](./Odysseus#cite_note-96)\\n\\nAccording to ancient Greek tradition, Odysseus founded a city in [Iberia](./Iberia \"Iberia\") which was called Odysseia (Ὀδύσσεια)[[97]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Strabo,_3.2.13-97)[[98]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Strabo,_3.4.3-98) or Odysseis (Ὀδυσσεῖς)[[99]](./Odysseus#cite_note-99) which had a sanctuary of goddess [Athena](./Athena \"Athena\").[[97]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Strabo,_3.2.13-97)[[98]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Strabo,_3.4.3-98)[[100]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Dictionary_of_Greek_and_Roman_Geography-100) Ancient authors identified it with [Olisipo](./Olisipo \"Olisipo\") (modern [Lisbon](./Lisbon \"Lisbon\")), but modern researchers believe that even its existence is uncertain.[[100]](./Odysseus#cite_note-Dictionary_of_Greek_and_Roman_Geography-100)\\n\\n[Hellanicus of Lesbos](./Hellanicus_of_Lesbos \"Hellanicus of Lesbos\") wrote that [Rome](./Rome \"Rome\") was founded by Aeneas and Odysseus who came together there. Other ancient historians, including [Damastes of Sigeum](./Damastes_of_Sigeum \"Damastes of Sigeum\"), agreed with him.[[101]](./Odysseus#cite_note-101)[[102]](./Odysseus#cite_note-102)\\n\\nNamesakes\\n---------\\n\\n* [Odysseus (crater)](./Odysseus_(crater) \"Odysseus (crater)\")\\n* [Prince Odysseas-Kimon of Greece and Denmark](./Prince_Odysseas-Kimon_of_Greece_and_Denmark \"Prince Odysseas-Kimon of Greece and Denmark\") (born 2004) is the grandson of the deposed Greek king, [Constantine II](./Constantine_II_of_the_Hellenes \"Constantine II of the Hellenes\").\\n* [1143 Odysseus](./1143_Odysseus \"1143 Odysseus\")\\n* [5254 Ulysses](./5254_Ulysses \"5254 Ulysses\")\\n* [IM-1](./IM-1 \"IM-1\")\\n\\nSee also\\n--------\\n\\n* *[Odysseus Unbound](./Odysseus_Unbound \"Odysseus Unbound\")*\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n1. Apology for Smectymnuus

Final antiprelatical tract by John Milton

|  |  |

| [icon](./File:Question_book-new.svg) | This article **relies excessively on [references](./Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability") to [primary sources](./Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")**. ***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

--------

* [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")

Telemachus

Mythological son of Odysseus

For other uses, see [Telemachus (disambiguation)](./Telemachus_(disambiguation) "Telemachus (disambiguation)").

Fictional character



| Telemachus | |
| --- | --- |
| Telemachus departing from Nestor, painting by [Henry Howard](./Henry_Howard_(artist) "Henry Howard (artist)") (1769–1847) | |
| In-universe information | |
| Title | Prince of Ithaca |
| Spouse | [Circe](./Circe "Circe");  or [Cassiphone](./Cassiphone "Cassiphone") or [Polycaste](./Polycaste "Polycaste") or [Nausicaa](./Nausicaa "Nausicaa") |
| Children | [Latinus](./Latinus "Latinus") [Persepolis](./Persepolis_(mythology) "Persepolis (mythology)") Ptoliporthus [Poliporthes](./Poliporthes "Poliporthes") |
| Relatives | [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") (father) [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") (mother) |
| Nationality | Greek |

**Telemachus** ([/təˈlɛməkəs/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Naomi_Persephone_Amethyst_(NaomiAmethyst)-Telemachus.wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Naomi Persephone Amethyst (NaomiAmethyst)-Telemachus.wav") [*tə-LEM-ə-kəs*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Τηλέμαχος, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Tēlemakhos*, [lit.](./Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'far-fighter') is the son of [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") and [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") in [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology"), and a central character in [Homer](./Homer "Homer")'s *[Odyssey](./Odyssey "Odyssey")*. When Telemachus reached manhood, he visited [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and [Sparta](./Sparta "Sparta") in search of his wandering father. On his return to [Ithaca](./Homer's_Ithaca "Homer's Ithaca"), he found that Odysseus had reached home before him. Then father and son slayed the [suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") who had gathered around to woo Penelope. According to later tradition, Telemachus married [Circe](./Circe "Circe") after Odysseus's death.

The first four books of the *Odyssey* focus on Telemachus's journeys in search of news about his father, who has yet to return home from the [Trojan War](./Trojan_War "Trojan War"), and are traditionally given the title *[Telemachy](./Telemachy "Telemachy")*.[[1]](./Telemachus#cite_note-1)

Etymology
---------

Telemachus's name in [Greek](./Greek_language "Greek language") means "far from battle", or perhaps "fighting from afar", as a bowman does.[[2]](./Telemachus#cite_note-2)

*Odyssey*
---------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Mnesterophonia_Louvre_CA7124.jpg/250px-Mnesterophonia_Louvre_CA7124.jpg)](./File:Mnesterophonia_Louvre_CA7124.jpg)

Slaughter of the suitors by Odysseus and Telemachus, [Campanian](./Campania "Campania") red-figure bell-[krater](./Krater "Krater"), ca. 330 BC, [Louvre](./Louvre "Louvre") (CA 7124)

In Homer's *Odyssey*, Telemachus, under the instructions of [Athena](./Athena "Athena") (who accompanies him during the quest), spends the first four books trying to gain knowledge of his father, Odysseus, who left for Troy when Telemachus was still an infant. At the outset of Telemachus's journey, Odysseus had been absent from his home at [Ithaca](./Homer's_Ithaca "Homer's Ithaca") for twenty years due to the Trojan War and the intervention of [Poseidon](./Poseidon "Poseidon"). During his absence, Odysseus's house has been occupied by hordes of suitors seeking the hand of Penelope.[[3]](./Telemachus#cite_note-3) Telemachus first visits [Nestor](./Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)") and is well received by the old man who regales him with stories of his father's glory. Telemachus then departs with Nestor's son [Peisistratus](./Peisistratus_(Odyssey) "Peisistratus (Odyssey)"),[[4]](./Telemachus#cite_note-4) who accompanies him to the halls of [Menelaus](./Menelaus "Menelaus") and his wife [Helen](./Helen_of_Troy "Helen of Troy"). While there, Telemachus is again treated as an honored guest as Menelaus and Helen tell complementary yet contradictory stories of his father's exploits at Troy. Telemachus also learns from Menelaus that his father was last seen stranded on [Ogygia](./Ogygia "Ogygia").[[5]](./Telemachus#cite_note-5)

Telemachus focuses on his father's [return to Ithaca](./Returns_from_Troy#The_Odyssey "Returns from Troy") in Book XV. He visits [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), the swineherd, who happens to be hosting a disguised Odysseus. After Odysseus reveals himself to Telemachus due to Athena's advice, the two men plan the downfall of the suitors. Telemachus then returns to the palace to keep an eye on the suitors and to await his father as the beggar.[[6]](./Telemachus#cite_note-6)

When Penelope challenges the suitors to string Odysseus's bow and shoot an arrow through the handle-holes of twelve axe heads, Telemachus is the first to attempt the task. He would have completed the task, nearly stringing the bow on his fourth attempt; however, Odysseus subtly stops him before he can finish his attempt. Following the suitors' failure at this task, Odysseus reveals himself and he and Telemachus bring swift and bloody death to the suitors.[[7]](./Telemachus#cite_note-7)

*Telegony*
----------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Telemachos_Saarbruecken.jpg/250px-Telemachos_Saarbruecken.jpg)](./File:Telemachos_Saarbruecken.jpg)

Statue depicting Telemachus

The *[Telegony](./Telegony "Telegony")* was a short two-book epic poem recounting the life and death of Odysseus after the events of the *Odyssey*. In this mythological postscript, Odysseus is accidentally killed by [Telegonus](./Telegonus_(son_of_Odysseus) "Telegonus (son of Odysseus)"), his unknown son by the goddess [Circe](./Circe "Circe"). After Odysseus's death, Telemachus returns to [Aeaea](./Aeaea "Aeaea") with Telegonus and Penelope, and there marries Circe.

Seemingly later tradition included the character of [Cassiphone](./Cassiphone "Cassiphone")—the daughter of Odysseus and Circe, and therefore half-sister of Telemachus—in the narrative. In this account, Telemachus still marries Circe, but Odysseus is resurrected by Circe at some point.

Later classical authors
-----------------------

From the *[Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology](./Dictionary_of_Greek_and_Roman_Biography_and_Mythology "Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology")*: In the post-Homeric traditions, we read that Palamedes, when endeavouring to persuade Odysseus to join the Greeks against Troy, and the latter feigned idiocy, placed the infant Telemachus before the plough with which Odysseus was ploughing.[[8]](./Telemachus#cite_note-8)

In *[Contest of Homer and Hesiod](./Contest_of_Homer_and_Hesiod "Contest of Homer and Hesiod")*, it is alleged that the Roman Emperor [Hadrian](./Hadrian "Hadrian") asked the [Delphic Oracle](./Delphic_Oracle "Delphic Oracle") about Homer's birthplace and parentage. The Oracle replied that Homer came from Ithaca and that Telemachus was his father by [Epicasta](./Epicasta "Epicasta"), daughter of Nestor.[[9]](./Telemachus#cite_note-9)[[10]](./Telemachus#cite_note-10)

According to [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle") and [Dictys of Crete](./Dictys_of_Crete "Dictys of Crete"), Telemachus married [Nausicaa](./Nausicaa "Nausicaa"), King Alcinous's daughter, and fathered a son named [Perseptolis](./Persepolis_(mythology) "Persepolis (mythology)") or [Ptoliporthus](./Poliporthes "Poliporthes").[[11]](./Telemachus#cite_note-11)

[Eustathius](./Eustathius_of_Thessalonica "Eustathius of Thessalonica") says that the mother was [Polycaste](./Polycaste "Polycaste"), the daughter of [Nestor](./Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)").[[12]](./Telemachus#cite_note-12) Others relate that he became the father of [Latinus](./Latinus "Latinus") by Circe.[[13]](./Telemachus#cite_note-13) He is also said to have had a daughter called Roma, who married [Aeneas](./Aeneas "Aeneas").[[14]](./Telemachus#cite_note-14)

Servius makes Telemachus the founder of the town of [Clusium](./Clusium "Clusium") in Etruria.[[15]](./Telemachus#cite_note-15)[[16]](./Telemachus#cite_note-16)

Other appearances
-----------------

Telemachus was the subject of numerous [operas](./Opera "Opera") throughout the eighteenth century, most based on Fénelon's version.[[17]](./Telemachus#cite_note-17) Among the most famous of these operas were [André Cardinal Destouches](./André_Cardinal_Destouches "André Cardinal Destouches")'s *[Télémaque](./Télémaque_(Destouches) "Télémaque (Destouches)")* (1714), [Alessandro Scarlatti](./Alessandro_Scarlatti "Alessandro Scarlatti")'s *[Telemaco](./Telemaco_(Scarlatti) "Telemaco (Scarlatti)")* (1718), Gluck's *[Telemaco, ossia L'isola di Circe](./Telemaco_(Gluck) "Telemaco (Gluck)")* (1765), [Giuseppe Gazzaniga](./Giuseppe_Gazzaniga "Giuseppe Gazzaniga")'s *Gli errori di Telemaco* (1776), [Jean-François Le Sueur](./Jean-François_Le_Sueur "Jean-François Le Sueur")'s *Télémaque dans l'île de Calypso ou Le triomphe de la sagesse* (1796), [Simon Mayr](./Simon_Mayr "Simon Mayr")'s *[Telemaco nell'isola di Calipso](./Telemaco_(Mayr) "Telemaco (Mayr)")* (1797), and Fernando Sor's *[Telemaco nell'isola di Calipso](./Telemaco_(Sor) "Telemaco (Sor)")* (1797).

[Les Aventures de Télémaque](./Les_Aventures_de_Télémaque "Les Aventures de Télémaque") is a novel by [François Fénelon](./François_Fénelon "François Fénelon").

Telemachus appears in Alfred, Lord Tennyson's 1833 poem "[Ulysses](./Ulysses_(poem) "Ulysses (poem)")", where the title speaker (based on Dante's version) hands over his throne to him to spend the rest of his life wandering.

Telemachus is a frequent character in the poetry of [Louise Glück](./Louise_Glück "Louise Glück").[[18]](./Telemachus#cite_note-18)

Telemachus was the name of [Carole King](./Carole_King "Carole King")'s cat and is pictured on the cover of her album *[Tapestry](./Tapestry_(Carole_King_album) "Tapestry (Carole King album)")*.[[19]](./Telemachus#cite_note-19)

"Telemachus" is the title of a poem by American poet [Ocean Vuong](./Ocean_Vuong "Ocean Vuong").[[20]](./Telemachus#cite_note-20)

Telemachus is featured in a musical adaptation of the *Odyssey* entitled *[Epic: The Musical](./Epic:_The_Musical "Epic: The Musical")*.

Telemachus

Mythological son of Odysseus

For other uses, see [Telemachus (disambiguation)](./Telemachus_(disambiguation) "Telemachus (disambiguation)").

Fictional character



| Telemachus | |
| --- | --- |
| Telemachus departing from Nestor, painting by [Henry Howard](./Henry_Howard_(artist) "Henry Howard (artist)") (1769–1847) | |
| In-universe information | |
| Title | Prince of Ithaca |
| Spouse | [Circe](./Circe "Circe");  or [Cassiphone](./Cassiphone "Cassiphone") or [Polycaste](./Polycaste "Polycaste") or [Nausicaa](./Nausicaa "Nausicaa") |
| Children | [Latinus](./Latinus "Latinus") [Persepolis](./Persepolis_(mythology) "Persepolis (mythology)") Ptoliporthus [Poliporthes](./Poliporthes "Poliporthes") |

**Telemachus** ([/təˈlɛməkəs/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Naomi_Persephone_Amethyst_(NaomiAmethyst)-Telemachus.wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Naomi Persephone Amethyst (NaomiAmethyst)-Telemachus.wav") [*tə-LEM-ə-kəs*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Τηλέμαχος, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Tēlemakhos*, [lit.](./Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'far-fighter') is the son of [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") and [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") in [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology"), and a central character in [Homer](./Homer "Homer")'s *[Odyssey](./Odyssey "Odyssey")*. When Telemachus reached manhood, he visited [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and [Sparta](./Sparta "Sparta") in search of his wandering father. On his return to [Ithaca](./Homer's_Ithaca "Homer's Ithaca"), he found that Odysseus had reached home before him. Then father and son slayed the [suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") who had gathered around to woo Penelope. According to later tradition, Telemachus married [Circe](./Circe "Circe") after Odysseus's death.

The first four books of the *Odyssey* focus on Telemachus's journeys in search of news about his father, who has yet to return home from the [Trojan War](./Trojan_War "Trojan War"), and are traditionally given the title *[Telemachy](./Telemachy "Telemachy")*.[[1]](./Telemachus#cite_note-1)

Etymology
---------

Telemachus's name in [Greek](./Greek_language "Greek language") means "far from battle", or perhaps "fighting from afar", as a bowman does.[[2]](./Telemachus#cite_note-2)

*Odyssey*
---------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Mnesterophonia_Louvre_CA7124.jpg/250px-Mnesterophonia_Louvre_CA7124.jpg)](./File:Mnesterophonia_Louvre_CA7124.jpg)

Slaughter of the suitors by Odysseus and Telemachus, [Campanian](./Campania "Campania") red-figure bell-[krater](./Krater "Krater"), ca. 330 BC, [Louvre](./Louvre "Louvre") (CA 7124)

In Homer's *Odyssey*, Telemachus, under the instructions of [Athena](./Athena "Athena") (who accompanies him during the quest), spends the first four books trying to gain knowledge of his father, Odysseus, who left for Troy when Telemachus was still an infant. At the outset of Telemachus's journey, Odysseus had been absent from his home at [Ithaca](./Homer's_Ithaca "Homer's Ithaca") for twenty years due to the Trojan War and the intervention of [Poseidon](./Poseidon "Poseidon"). During his absence, Odysseus's house has been occupied by hordes of suitors seeking the hand of Penelope.[[3]](./Telemachus#cite_note-3) Telemachus first visits [Nestor](./Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)") and is well received by the old man who regales him with stories of his father's glory. Telemachus then departs with Nestor's son [Peisistratus](./Peisistratus_(Odyssey) "Peisistratus (Odyssey)"),[[4]](./Telemachus#cite_note-4) who accompanies him to the halls of [Menelaus](./Menelaus "Menelaus") and his wife [Helen](./Helen_of_Troy "Helen of Troy"). While there, Telemachus is again treated as an honored guest as Menelaus and Helen tell complementary yet contradictory stories of his father's exploits at Troy. Telemachus also learns from Menelaus that his father was last seen stranded on [Ogygia](./Ogygia "Ogygia").[[5]](./Telemachus#cite_note-5)

Telemachus focuses on his father's [return to Ithaca](./Returns_from_Troy#The_Odyssey "Returns from Troy") in Book XV. He visits [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), the swineherd, who happens to be hosting a disguised Odysseus. After Odysseus reveals himself to Telemachus due to Athena's advice, the two men plan the downfall of the suitors. Telemachus then returns to the palace to keep an eye on the suitors and to await his father as the beggar.[[6]](./Telemachus#cite_note-6)

When Penelope challenges the suitors to string Odysseus's bow and shoot an arrow through the handle-holes of twelve axe heads, Telemachus is the first to attempt the task. He would have completed the task, nearly stringing the bow on his fourth attempt; however, Odysseus subtly stops him before he can finish his attempt. Following the suitors' failure at this task, Odysseus reveals himself and he and Telemachus bring swift and bloody death to the suitors.[[7]](./Telemachus#cite_note-7)

*Telegony*
----------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Telemachos_Saarbruecken.jpg/250px-Telemachos_Saarbruecken.jpg)](./File:Telemachos_Saarbruecken.jpg)

Statue depicting Telemachus

The *[Telegony](./Telegony "Telegony")* was a short two-book epic poem recounting the life and death of Odysseus after the events of the *Odyssey*. In this mythological postscript, Odysseus is accidentally killed by [Telegonus](./Telegonus_(son_of_Odysseus) "Telegonus (son of Odysseus)"), his unknown son by the goddess [Circe](./Circe "Circe"). After Odysseus's death, Telemachus returns to [Aeaea](./Aeaea "Aeaea") with Telegonus and Penelope, and there marries Circe.

Seemingly later tradition included the character of [Cassiphone](./Cassiphone "Cassiphone")—the daughter of Odysseus and Circe, and therefore half-sister of Telemachus—in the narrative. In this account, Telemachus still marries Circe, but Odysseus is resurrected by Circe at some point.

Later classical authors
-----------------------

From the *[Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology](./Dictionary_of_Greek_and_Roman_Biography_and_Mythology "Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology")*: In the post-Homeric traditions, we read that Palamedes, when endeavouring to persuade Odysseus to join the Greeks against Troy, and the latter feigned idiocy, placed the infant Telemachus before the plough with which Odysseus was ploughing.[[8]](./Telemachus#cite_note-8)

In *[Contest of Homer and Hesiod](./Contest_of_Homer_and_Hesiod "Contest of Homer and Hesiod")*, it is alleged that the Roman Emperor [Hadrian](./Hadrian "Hadrian") asked the [Delphic Oracle](./Delphic_Oracle "Delphic Oracle") about Homer's birthplace and parentage. The Oracle replied that Homer came from Ithaca and that Telemachus was his father by [Epicasta](./Epicasta "Epicasta"), daughter of Nestor.[[9]](./Telemachus#cite_note-9)[[10]](./Telemachus#cite_note-10)

According to [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle") and [Dictys of Crete](./Dictys_of_Crete "Dictys of Crete"), Telemachus married [Nausicaa](./Nausicaa "Nausicaa"), King Alcinous's daughter, and fathered a son named [Perseptolis](./Persepolis_(mythology) "Persepolis (mythology)") or [Ptoliporthus](./Poliporthes "Poliporthes").[[11]](./Telemachus#cite_note-11)

[Eustathius](./Eustathius_of_Thessalonica "Eustathius of Thessalonica") says that the mother was [Polycaste](./Polycaste "Polycaste"), the daughter of [Nestor](./Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)").[[12]](./Telemachus#cite_note-12) Others relate that he became the father of [Latinus](./Latinus "Latinus") by Circe.[[13]](./Telemachus#cite_note-13) He is also said to have had a daughter called Roma, who married [Aeneas](./Aeneas "Aeneas").[[14]](./Telemachus#cite_note-14)

Servius makes Telemachus the founder of the town of [Clusium](./Clusium "Clusium") in Etruria.[[15]](./Telemachus#cite_note-15)[[16]](./Telemachus#cite_note-16)

Other appearances
-----------------

Telemachus was the subject of numerous [operas](./Opera "Opera") throughout the eighteenth century, most based on Fénelon's version.[[17]](./Telemachus#cite_note-17) Among the most famous of these operas were [André Cardinal Destouches](./André_Cardinal_Destouches "André Cardinal Destouches")'s *[Télémaque](./Télémaque_(Destouches) "Télémaque (Destouches)")* (1714), [Alessandro Scarlatti](./Alessandro_Scarlatti "Alessandro Scarlatti")'s *[Telemaco](./Telemaco_(Scarlatti) "Telemaco (Scarlatti)")* (1718), Gluck's *[Telemaco, ossia L'isola di Circe](./Telemaco_(Gluck) "Telemaco (Gluck)")* (1765), [Giuseppe Gazzaniga](./Giuseppe_Gazzaniga "Giuseppe Gazzaniga")'s *Gli errori di Telemaco* (1776), [Jean-François Le Sueur](./Jean-François_Le_Sueur "Jean-François Le Sueur")'s *Télémaque dans l'île de Calypso ou Le triomphe de la sagesse* (1796), [Simon Mayr](./Simon_Mayr "Simon Mayr")'s *[Telemaco nell'isola di Calipso](./Telemaco_(Mayr) "Telemaco (Mayr)")* (1797), and Fernando Sor's *[Telemaco nell'isola di Calipso](./Telemaco_(Sor) "Telemaco (Sor)")* (1797).

[Les Aventures de Télémaque](./Les_Aventures_de_Télémaque "Les Aventures de Télémaque") is a novel by [François Fénelon](./François_Fénelon "François Fénelon").

Telemachus appears in Alfred, Lord Tennyson's 1833 poem "[Ulysses](./Ulysses_(poem) "Ulysses (poem)")", where the title speaker (based on Dante's version) hands over his throne to him to spend the rest of his life wandering.

Telemachus is a frequent character in the poetry of [Louise Glück](./Louise_Glück "Louise Glück").[[18]](./Telemachus#cite_note-18)

Telemachus was the name of [Carole King](./Carole_King "Carole King")'s cat and is pictured on the cover of her album *[Tapestry](./Tapestry_(Carole_King_album) "Tapestry (Carole King album)")*.[[19]](./Telemachus#cite_note-19)

"Telemachus" is the title of a poem by American poet [Ocean Vuong](./Ocean_Vuong "Ocean Vuong").[[20]](./Telemachus#cite_note-20)

Telemachus is featured in a musical adaptation of the *Odyssey* entitled *[Epic: The Musical](./Epic:_The_Musical "Epic: The Musical")*.

Apology for Smectymnuus

Final antiprelatical tract by John Milton

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Dryope (daughter of Dryops)

Daughter of Dryops or of Eurytus, mother of Amphissus

For other uses, see [Dryope](./Dryope "Dryope").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Dr%C3%ADope_transformada_em_l%C3%B3tus.jpg/250px-Dr%C3%ADope_transformada_em_l%C3%B3tus.jpg)](./File:Dríope_transformada_em_lótus.jpg)

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology"), **Dryope** ([/ˈdraɪ.əpiː/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Δρυόπη) is the daughter of [Dryops, king of Oeta](./Dryops_(Oeta) "Dryops (Oeta)") ("oak-man")[[1]](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops)#cite_note-:0-1) or of [Eurytus](./Eurytus,_king_of_Oechalia "Eurytus, king of Oechalia") (and hence half-sister to [Iole](./Iole "Iole")).[[2]](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops)#cite_note-:1-2) Dryope mothered [Amphissus](./Amphissus "Amphissus") by [Apollo](./Apollo "Apollo").[[1]](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops)#cite_note-:0-1)

Mythology
---------

There is a story of her [metamorphosis](./Shapeshifting "Shapeshifting") into a [black poplar](./Black_poplar "Black poplar"), and a story of her changing into a lotus tree.

### Antoninus Liberalis' account

According to the first, Apollo seduced her by a trick. While Dryope tended the flocks of her father on Mount Oeta, she became the playmate of the [hamadryads](./Hamadryad "Hamadryad") of the woods on [Mount Oeta](./Mount_Oeta "Mount Oeta"). The nymphs taught her to sing hymns to the gods and to dance. On one occasion, Dryope was seen by Apollo. In order to win her favours the god turned himself into a [tortoise](./Tortoise "Tortoise"), of which the girls made a pet. The nymphs played with the animal and when Dryope had the tortoise on her lap, Apollo turned into a snake. The nymphs then got scared and abandoned her, and Apollo raped her. Eventually she gave birth to her son Amphissus. Soon afterwards Dryope married [Andraemon](./Andraemon "Andraemon"), son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus"). Amphissus eventually built a temple to his father Apollo in the city of Oeta, which he founded. Here the nymphs came to converse with Dryope, who had become a priestess of the temple. Fond of her, they took her with them and placed a poplar tree in her place. They then turned her into a nymph. Two [women](./Oechalides "Oechalides") of the town told the people that the nymphs had taken Dryope, so the nymphs turned them into fir trees.[[3]](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops)#cite_note-3)

### Ovid's account

In [Ovid](./Ovid "Ovid")'s version of the story,[[2]](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops)#cite_note-:1-2) Dryope was wandering by a lake, suckling her baby Amphissus, when she saw the bright red flowers of the lotus, formerly the nymph [Lotis](./Lotis_(mythology) "Lotis (mythology)") who, when fleeing from [Priapus](./Priapus "Priapus"), had been changed into a tree. Dryope wanted to give the blossoms to her baby to play with, but when she picked one the tree started to tremble and bleed. She tried to run away, but the blood of the tree had touched her skin and she found her feet rooted to the spot. She slowly began to turn into a lotus tree, the bark spreading up her legs from the earth, but just before the woody stiffness finally reached her throat and as her arms began sprouting twigs her husband Andraemon heard her cries and came to her. She had just enough time to warn her husband to take care of their child and make sure that he did not pick flowers. She also told him to find Amphissus a nurse and to tell him to call her his mother.

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)
